explanation:
## The program

```cpp
void extremes(const std::vector<int>& values, int& lowest, int& highest)
{
    lowest = values[0];
    highest = values[0];

    for (std::size_t i = 1; i < values.size(); ++i)
    {
        if (values[i] < lowest)  lowest = values[i];
        if (values[i] > highest) highest = values[i];
    }
}
```

## Three parameters, three different jobs

```
const std::vector<int>&   read it, do not copy it, do not change it
int&                      this is where an answer goes
int&                      and here is the other one
```

Reading a declaration like that tells you how the function is used
before you look at the body, which is most of the value of the
convention. A `const&` is an input; a plain `&` is an output or an
in-out; a by-value parameter is an input small enough not to care.

## What const buys

Two things, and the second matters more than it looks.

**It stops the copy from being needed.** Without the `&` the whole
vector is duplicated on every call. For 10,000 `int`s that is 40 KB
of memcpy per call, for nothing.

**It is checked.** Add `values.push_back(0);` inside the function
and it will not compile. A promise the compiler enforces is worth
more than a comment saying the same thing, and this is the cheapest
such promise in the language.

## Starting from the first element

The same running-minimum question as before, answered by the
caller: the function is only ever called on a non-empty vector, so
`values[0]` exists and is a legitimate starting value for both
answers. The loop then starts at index 1, since element 0 has
already been accounted for.

That guarantee is a **precondition**, and it lives in the caller.
Letting the function cope instead — by returning early, or writing
zeros — would mean the caller could not tell "the minimum is 0"
from "there was nothing". Keeping it out, and printing `empty`
before the call, keeps both answers honest.

A library version would take the question seriously:
`std::minmax_element` returns iterators, and on an empty range it
returns the end iterator, which the caller must check. Same problem,
same shape of answer.

## Two results without references

Modern C++ has other ways:

```cpp
std::pair<int, int> extremes(const std::vector<int>& v);
auto [lo, hi] = extremes(values);           // structured bindings
```

which reads better at the call site and is usually preferred now.
Reference out-parameters are still everywhere in existing code, and
are the form that needs understanding first.

## What this does not check

What the function does when its precondition is broken. Calling
`extremes` on an empty vector reads `values[0]`, which is undefined
behaviour — it will not throw, and it may well print a plausible
number. A defensive version would `assert(!values.empty())`, which
documents the requirement and checks it in debug builds.
